bibliography.abstract: Marriage migration does not end mobility; it often reorganises it. Based on 8 months of multi-sited ethnography in Ethiopia and China, supplemented by digital follow-up through WeChat, this article examines how marriage migration produced destination-country immobility for Ethiopian wives in rural China. After arrival, women often became isolated and dependent within multigenerational households, where language barriers, racialised visibility, and marriage-based residence constrained mobility and intensified surveillance. I argue that this immobilisation was maintained and unevenly reopened through a post-arrival infrastructure linking legal, domestic-relational, digital-technological, and practical-mobility arrangements. Extending Miller’s notion of the ‘death of proximity’, the article shows how physical co-residence with husbands and affinal kin did not guarantee intimacy or incorporation. Within this post-arrival infrastructure, smartphones provided access to a portable elsewhere: through WeChat, women located peers, exchanged practical and sometimes mistaken information, sustained mediated co-presence beyond the village household, and shared scripts for relocating to Chinese cities. These affordances reconfigured the limited and risky conditions under which endurance, planning, and re-mobility became possible.
bibliography.title: Portable elsewhere: re-mobility, marriage migration, and the ‘death of proximity’ among Ethiopian wives in China

en.caveats: The findings are based on qualitative ethnographic methods and digital tracking of a specific migrant corridor, which may not represent the dynamics of marriage migration in other national contexts.
en.what: Based on an eight-month multi-sited ethnography in Ethiopia and China alongside digital follow-up on WeChat, this study documents how Ethiopian wives in rural China experience severe destination-country immobility within multigenerational households. It details how language barriers, racialized visibility, and marriage-based residency rules restrict their movement, and how these women use smartphones to access a 'portable elsewhere' to coordinate survival strategies and plan relocation to Chinese cities.
en.why: The study demonstrates that physical co-residence does not guarantee social integration, showing instead how digital infrastructures like WeChat allow marginalized migrants to bypass physical isolation and organize secondary migration within the host country.
